transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-07-07
Time: 09:00 UTC (09:00–09:52)
Duration: 52 minutes
Attendees: Maya Patel (Redwood AE), Jonas Chen (Redwood SE), Leah Ortiz (Redwood CSM), Dr. Amir Hassan (TidalHealth CTO), Laura Kim (TidalHealth VP Eng), Samir Patel (TidalHealth SRE), Nina Torres (Product)

Summary: quick recap of last-week outage (token surge + KV cache evictions), preliminary RCA items, proposed short-term mitigations (sticky routing + throttled backlog), and rollforward plan to run a Dedicated soak and validation harness.
Topics: incident timeline, telemetry gaps, mitigation options, runbook/rollback phone tree, pilot schedule.
Action items (as captured): see metadata.

--- Transcript ---
[00:00] Maya Patel: OK, good morning everyone, thanks for making time. We want to keep this tight, we have 50-ish minutes. Quick rollcall?
[00:08] Dr. Amir Hassan: Amir here, hi.
[00:10] Laura Kim: Laura, hi.
[00:11] Samir Patel: Samir.
[00:12] Nina Torres: Nina.
[00:13] Jonas Chen: Jonas from Redwood.
[00:15] Leah Ortiz: Leah here.
[00:17] Maya Patel: Great. Quick agenda: one, recap of what we saw last Thursday; two, what we've validated so far; three, short-term mitigations; four, rollforward plan and who owns what. Sound OK?
[00:27] Laura Kim: Sounds good. We mostly want to understand the RCA and get a plan to prevent recurrence.
[00:32] Maya Patel: Totally. So quick recap, high level — around 14:12 UTC on Thursday your production route hit a token surge from a bad batch job which led to request chaining, the K V cache — our logs show repeated evictions, and that increased GPU load and degraded scheduling which created a backlog. That backlog, combined with autoscale lag, caused tail latency to balloon and then failover to a fallback model occurred and churned resources.
[00:56] Amir Hassan: Two clarifications: the batch job was a data export that kicked off unexpectedly, right? And you saw both prefix cache evictions and full KV rehydration?
[01:05] Jonas Chen: Yes, our traces show evictions starting ~14:14; we saw high cache miss rates and repeated kv-reauthorization calls — sometimes transcribed as K V uh cash in the raw logs — which forced the runtime to reload large KV sets. That produced a lot of small allocations and pinned GPU memory for several seconds per request.
[01:26] Samir Patel: We also saw the requests from the job hit the realtime endpoints not the async path because of an incorrect header in the job config. That was our fault on the client side but it exposed an autoscale and routing gap.
[01:36] Maya Patel: Good, appreciate the callout. So root causes are a mix: client misconfiguration (sync vs async), unexpected token-volume spike, and then systemic vulnerabilities in the routing/autoscale window plus insufficient early throttling at the edge.
[01:49] Nina Torres: One thing we care about is data retention — we were worried logs might expose PHI, are the spans redacted?
[01:56] Jonas Chen: Short answer, the spans we will share are sanitized. We'll strip PII/PHI before pushing the zip; that's part of the RCA artifact.
[02:04] Laura Kim: Ok good. Can you walk through the timeline with the tail numbers?
[02:08] Jonas Chen: Sure, brief numbers: the surge started at 14:12, 14:14 cache misses increased from baseline 2% to 48% over five minutes, GPU utilization went from 65% to sustained 95% at 14:17, scheduler queue length increased 12x, and error rates peaked ~14:22. Our internal fallback kicked in at 14:23. We have the traces and flame graphs but there are some telemetry gaps around 14:16–14:18 due to dropped agent heartbeats; we have partial logs from the node.
[02:36] Samir Patel: That 14:16 gap is the one we were worried about — our sidecar crashed under memory pressure at that time, so we lost some application-level metrics.
[02:44] Leah Ortiz: OK we'll annotate the RCA to call out those telemetry blind spots.
[02:48] Maya Patel: Now fixes. Short-term mitigations (minutes-to-hours): 1) apply a conservative edge-rate limit for that customer route, 2) enable sticky routing to a Dedicated pool where possible, 3) temporarily increase KV cache size or adjust eviction policy to prefer prefix caching for your prompt shapes, 4) avoid fallback model warm startup churn by pre-warming lighter variants. These are stopgaps while we do the deeper work.
[03:15] Laura Kim: Sticky routing to Dedicated sounds attractive but we need to understand cost implications.
[03:19] Maya Patel: Absolutely. Sticky does increase cost because Dedicated capacity is reserved; for a short pilot we'll propose a small Dedicated allocation for the high-risk route only. We'll put numbers in the follow-up pricing note.
[03:29] Jonas Chen: Technical note: sticky routing will avoid hitting the general shared pool which is the area where the autoscaler lag compounded. Also we can tune autoscale policy — shorten the aggregation window and add an emergency scale trigger on sustained queue depth.
[03:45] Laura Kim: On the KV side, is that a config flag we can change from our side or a Redwood change?
[03:50] Jonas Chen: There's a client-side parameter that controls prefix retention hints — you can set a stronger hints value in the SDK config. But we also suggest a runtime fallback that prefers prefix retention for known prompt families. That needs a small runtime deployment (SE-led).
[04:05] Maya Patel: For the mid-term items (days-weeks): 1) add a client-side validation to prevent realtime header misuse in scheduled jobs (we can provide a snippet), 2) run the regression harness in staging (we'll provide a load script), 3) tweak autoscale windows and deployment of pre-warmed lighter model variants, and 4) enable more granular tracing to remove telemetry blind spots.
[04:25] Samir Patel: About the validation, can Redwood provide a pre-commit or CI check? We want something that fails the job config before it reaches prod.
[04:32] Leah Ortiz: Yes we can share a CI hook and a policy snippet for your infra team. We'll include a PR text you can paste.
[04:37] Nina Torres: For compliance audit, we will need the sanitized logs and also the timeline artifact for our internal review.
[04:43] Maya Patel: We'll push a sanitized RCA bundle by Friday 2026-07-09. It will contain timelines, sanitized spans, flamegraphs, and the list of mitigation toggles.
[04:52] Laura Kim: On the rollforward plan: what does a Dedicated soak look like operationally?
[04:57] Jonas Chen: Good question. For the pilot we'll provision a small Dedicated pool (2–4 GPUs depending on your model footprint), route a percentage of production traffic to it, and run a 7-day soak with gradual ramping and synthetic traffic that mirrors last week's spike. We'll monitor queue depth, cache hit ratio, tail latency, and memory fragmentation.
[05:17] Amir Hassan: Is there an automated fallback if the Dedicated pool shows similar contention?
[05:21] Jonas Chen: We'll set an automatic fallback policy that sends traffic back to a safe, lighter variant in the hosted pool. But the goal is to avoid that by pre-warming and better cache hints.
[05:29] Laura Kim: Cost and timeline — we need Redwood's estimate for a 7-day pilot and the test harness before we sign off.
[05:35] Maya Patel: We'll include a cost estimate in the follow-up email. Expect three parts: Dedicated reservation cost pro-rata for 7 days, engineering time for pre-warm/runtime change (Jonas estimate), and our support hours.
[05:47] Samir Patel: Operationally, who owns the rollback if things get worse during soak? We need a clear phone tree.
[05:53] Maya Patel: Leah will own the incident channel and coordination; Jonas will own the technical rollback steps and we'll all be on the call. We'll document the exact rollback commands and the person authorized to execute them.
[06:03] Leah Ortiz: I'll create the incident channel right after this call and invite TidalHealth ops; action item assigned.
[06:08] Nina Torres: A question about longtail errors — we saw a class of 503s correlated with specific prompt lengths. Is that something you can tune?
[06:16] Jonas Chen: Yes, often it's due to kv cache fragmentation for long context. We can profile and suggest quantization or chunking strategies for those prompt families. There's also a storage layer compaction we can trigger.
[06:28] Laura Kim: Is there a risk that compaction will itself cause a short-term CPU/GPU spike?
[06:33] Jonas Chen: It can, so we'll schedule compaction during low traffic windows and throttle compaction IO.
[06:38] Maya Patel: Ok, getting close to time. Let's recap next steps and owners: Redwood to send sanitized RCA + span logs (Maya), Jonas to attach flamegraphs and PR for autoscale tweaks, Leah to create incident channel and coordinate pilot schedule, Samir to run staging reproduction and share load script. And we agreed on a follow-up 30-min sync on 2026-07-16 to review soak results and sign off on rollforward.
[06:58] Amir Hassan: That all sounds good. One last ask — can Redwood include SLO targets for the pilot (latency p95/p99) so we can evaluate?
[07:06] Maya Patel: Yes we'll propose SLOs in the follow-up note. Expect p95 < 300ms and p99 < 1.2s as a starting target for the Dedicated pilot, but we'll adjust based on your baseline.
[07:19] Laura Kim: Thanks. Also please include the suppression thresholds so we know when to escalate automatically.
[07:24] Jonas Chen: We'll add queue depth thresholds and cache-miss triggers.
[07:27] Maya Patel: Great. Any final questions?
[07:30] Samir Patel: None from me.
[07:31] Nina Torres: No.
[07:31] Laura Kim: No.
[07:32] Maya Patel: OK, we'll follow up with the RCA and the pricing note. Thanks everyone, we'll be in touch.
[07:36] (meeting ends)
